conditions.label: Neurogenic bladder
conditions.note: Underactive bladder from diabetic autonomic neuropathy

conditions.label: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic autonomic (poly)neuropathy

documents.title: Urology Consultation
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY CONSULTATION
Visit date: 01/19/2024
Patient: Philip Hall, 67-year-old man
Referring: primary care
Reason: difficulty voiding, night-time leakage

Dear Doctor,

Thank you for sending Mr. Hall. He has had type 2 diabetes for close to three decades, poorly controlled, with peripheral neuropathy and retinopathy, as well as stage 3b CKD and a history of B12 deficiency on replacement.

History: over roughly the past year he has found it steadily harder to start his stream. The flow is weak and intermittent, and he dribbles after he believes he has finished. At times he feels the need to go but cannot get the bladder to empty. For the last several weeks he has woken at night with damp underwear, unaware of having leaked. He denies dysuria, suprapubic pain, fevers and blood in the urine. He admits he has missed a number of medical appointments over the past year.

Medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, insulin glargine 30 units nightly, lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg. Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol; retired from the postal service.
Family: father with type 2 diabetes; mother with gastric adenocarcinoma; maternal grandfather with colon cancer.

Exam: the bladder can be felt above the pubic bone and is mildly tender to percussion. External genitalia normal. DRE: prostate about 25 g, smooth, no nodules. Focused neurologic exam: reduced sensation in both lower extremities, ankle jerks diminished on both sides.

Bladder scan after an attempted void: post-void residual 360 mL. UA and PSA from your office normal.

Impression: incomplete bladder emptying with overflow leakage from a neurogenic, poorly contracting bladder. With no history of spinal or pelvic injury, the most likely cause is diabetic autonomic neuropathy affecting the sacral nerve supply to the bladder. The prostate is not enlarged.

Plan:
- Drained in clinic by straight catheter.
- Clean intermittent self-catheterization four times daily, taught today by our nurse with good return demonstration. Hydrophilic 14 Fr catheters; supply order sent (may need a prior authorization from your office).
- Timed voiding before each catheterization. Avoid anticholinergic medications.
- Return in about 4 months with catheterization volume diary.

Urology

documents.title: Prior auth: intermittent catheters
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Medical supply company called: hydrophilic intermittent catheters (14 Fr, 120/month) need documentation of neurogenic bladder and PVR. Faxed urology consult 1/19 (PVR 360 mL) and signed order. Called pt: he has been using the starter pack from urology and has enough for about a week. Approval came back same afternoon; first shipment out tomorrow. Pt says catheterizing "is not fun but I can do it."

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up: Neurogenic Bladder, Diabetes
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Urology letter from January reviewed: neurogenic bladder from diabetic autonomic neuropathy, PVR 360, started on self-catheterization.

He is catheterizing four times a day. Took about two weeks to get comfortable. Night wetting stopped. Stream still weak when he tries to void first. No fever, no burning, no cloudy urine. Supplies arriving monthly.

Exam: abdomen soft, no suprapubic fullness. Heart regular, lungs clear. Feet intact.

A/P:
1. Neurogenic bladder: doing well with CIC. Reviewed UTI warning signs. Urology follow-up in May.
2. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy added to problem list. Reminder that this, too, is a reason to bring sugars down; he nods but declines a change today.
3. DM2: A1c was 9.0 in December; next draw August.
4. HTN: BP fine today. Continue lisinopril.

documents.title: Urology Follow-up
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
Re: Philip Hall, DOB 07/22/1956. Seen 05/21/2024.

Mr. Hall returns four months after starting clean intermittent catheterization. Diary shows four catheterizations a day with volumes of 250 to 350 mL. Night-time wetting has resolved. No UTIs. No hematuria, no difficulty passing the catheter.

Abdomen soft, bladder not palpable.

Assessment: neurogenic bladder due to diabetic autonomic neuropathy, well managed with CIC.
Plan: continue CIC four times daily. Return in 12 months or sooner with fever, blood in the urine or trouble catheterizing.

Urology. Allergies: NKDA.

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual wellness, 68M.

Interval: urology in May, CIC going well, continue. He did not get to nephrology this year (appointment in January was missed and not rebooked); will ask the front desk to reschedule. Eye exam overdue since July.

Functional: independent. No falls. Drives in daylight. Wife helps with the monthly B12 shot.
PHQ-9: 3, mostly sleep interruptions he attributes to the night catheterization.
Cognition: intact on screen.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, glargine 30 qhs, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg IM monthly; intermittent catheters. NKDA.

Exam: well. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no bladder distension. No edema. Feet: skin intact, monofilament reduced at toes, pulses present.

Plan:
- Labs today.
- Fall vaccines: high-dose flu and RSV vaccine (age with diabetes and CKD) in late September; COVID at pharmacy.
- Rebook nephrology and eye exam.
- Diabetes visit in November.

documents.title: Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Philip, your A1c is 9.3. Creatinine 1.95, a little higher than last year but within the range we've seen; I'd still like you to see nephrology this year, the front desk will call with a date. Blood count normal. Cholesterol on target. Urine protein normal.

documents.title: Nurse Visit: Flu and RSV
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Screened, no contraindications. High-dose influenza (trivalent) 0.5 mL IM L deltoid. Arexvy 0.5 mL IM R deltoid. VIS for both. Observed 15 min without reaction. Pt reports catheterizing without problems.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Diabetes Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Feeling well. Has been more careful with portions since the summer labs, he says. Fasting 140s-190s. No lows. CIC 4x/day, no infections. Nephrology booked for March, eye exam booked for January.

O: no distress. Heart regular, lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Feet: skin intact, no fissures or calluses; monofilament reduced at toes.

A1c 8.9.

A/P: DM2, A1c 8.9, slightly better. Offered once again to adjust glargine; declines. Continue all meds. Next visit spring.

documents.title: Ophthalmology Letter
documents.author: ophthalmology
documents.body:
Dear Doctor,

Philip Hall (DOB 07/22/1956) was seen 01/09/2025 for his diabetic eye examination, about 18 months after his last visit.

VA cc 20/30 OU. IOP 15/16. Dilated fundus exam and photographs: diabetic retinopathy in both eyes, unchanged from July 2023. OCT: no macular edema either eye.

Impression: diabetic retinopathy OU, stable, without macular edema.
Recommendation: annual exam, please encourage him to keep it.

NKDA. Thank you.

documents.title: Nephrology Follow-up Letter
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Nephrology follow-up, 03/18/2025
Re: Philip Hall

Dear Doctor,

Mr. Hall returns after two years (his 2024 visit was missed). Since we last saw him he was diagnosed with a neurogenic bladder by urology and performs intermittent self-catheterization, which has gone well. No UTIs. He feels well.

Meds: metformin, insulin glargine, lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, monthly B12. NKDA.

BP acceptable today, no edema.
Labs today: creatinine 1.91 mg/dL, potassium 5.0.

Assessment: CKD G3b, stable over three years. Potassium high-normal on lisinopril with dietary modification. Bladder drainage by CIC is important for protecting his kidneys and he understands this.
Plan: continue current regimen and dietary potassium precautions. Labs with PCP twice a year. Return in 12 months.

Nephrology
